string-array.name: facts_animals
string-array.item: A blue whale\'s heart can weigh around 400 pounds (180 kg) — about as much as an upright piano.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the algae and tiny crustaceans they eat.
Sea otters sometimes hold hands while sleeping so they don\'t drift apart.
Some snails can remain dormant for up to three years during long dry periods.
Elephants cannot jump, but they can walk surprisingly quietly for their size.
A ruby-throated hummingbird\'s heart can beat more than 1,200 times per minute in flight.
Cows form preferred friendships and can become stressed when separated from their companions.
Giant tortoises can live for more than 150 years.
Koala fingerprints look remarkably similar to human fingerprints.
Butterflies taste with their feet.
A shrimp\'s heart is located in its cephalothorax, where its head and chest are fused together.
Polar bears have black skin beneath fur that looks white but is actually translucent.
A woodpecker can peck a tree up to 20 times per second.
Kangaroos cannot easily move backward because of their large feet and powerful tail.
The tongue of a giraffe can be up to 20 inches (50 cm) long.
Sea stars have no brain or heart; a water vascular system powers their many tube feet.
An ostrich\'s eye is bigger than its brain.
Dolphins recognize one another by unique signature whistles.
A cheetah can go from 0 to 60 mph in about 3 seconds.
Some wood frogs survive winter even when much of the water in their bodies freezes.
A membrane holds a crocodile\'s tongue in place, so it cannot stick it out.
Honeybees can learn to distinguish patterns that resemble human faces.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived on Earth.
Some ants can carry objects 50 times their own body weight.
A newborn giant panda is pink, nearly hairless, and about 1/900 the size of its mother.
Axolotls can regrow lost limbs, including bones, muscles, nerves, and skin.
Electric eels can generate shocks of up to about 860 volts.
Adélie penguins build nests from pebbles and carefully guard the stones they collect.

string-array.name: facts_space
string-array.item: Venus takes longer to rotate once on its axis than to complete one orbit around the Sun.
The footprints left by astronauts on the Moon will stay there for millions of years — there\'s no wind to blow them away.
One million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
Saturn\'s average density is lower than water, so it could float in an ocean large enough to hold it.
A neutron star is so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tons.
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
The vacuum of space is silent because it has no medium to carry sound waves.
Jupiter has the shortest day of all the planets — it spins all the way around in about 10 hours.
Some red supergiant stars have diameters more than 1,000 times that of the Sun.
On Mars, the sky near the setting Sun looks blue instead of orange.
An entire year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.
Astronauts can temporarily grow up to 2 inches (5 cm) taller in space because their spine stretches out.
Jupiter\'s Great Red Spot is a giant storm that astronomers have observed for at least 150 years.
The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth — about 1.5 inches (3.8 cm) every year.
Walking nonstop at 3 mph (5 km/h) would take almost nine years to reach the Moon.
The International Space Station travels around the Earth 16 times every single day.
Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
A cloud of gas and dust called a nebula can span hundreds of light-years.
Driving nonstop at 60 mph (about 100 km/h) would take roughly 177 years to reach the Sun.
Saturn\'s rings are made mostly of ice and rock, and some pieces are as small as a grain of sugar.
The Sun makes up about 99.8% of all the mass in our entire solar system.
Some planets beyond our solar system orbit two stars at once.
Mercury has only a thin exosphere, so its surface is scorching by day and freezing at night.
Black holes don\'t actually \"suck\" things in — objects fall toward them because of gravity, just like on Earth.
In microgravity, a massive object is still hard to stop once it starts moving because it keeps its inertia.
Our solar system lies in the Orion Spur, a small branch between two of the Milky Way\'s main spiral arms.
In microgravity, a candle flame becomes nearly spherical instead of teardrop-shaped.
Uranus\'s axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so the planet rotates almost on its side.
Apollo astronauts left reflectors on the Moon that scientists still use to measure its distance from Earth.
Comets are sometimes called \"dirty snowballs\" because they\'re made of ice, dust, and rock.

string-array.name: facts_dinosaurs
string-array.item: Some dinosaurs, like Velociraptor, were actually about the size of a turkey — not giant like in movies!
The word \"dinosaur\" means \"terrible lizard\" in Greek.
Argentinosaurus may have weighed as much as 10 elephants.
Some dinosaurs had feathers, just like birds today.
Modern birds are the only dinosaurs that survived the mass extinction 66 million years ago.
A Tyrannosaurus rex tooth, including its root, could be about as long as a banana.
Stegosaurus had two rows of large plates along its back and four spikes on its tail.
Some fossil dinosaur eggs are more than 18 inches (45 cm) long.
Spinosaurus had a long, crocodile-like snout and conical teeth suited to catching fish.
Triceratops had one of the largest skulls of any land animal ever, up to 8 feet (2.4 m) long.
Non-avian dinosaurs lived on Earth for over 165 million years, until the mass extinction 66 million years ago.
Not all giant prehistoric creatures were dinosaurs — flying pterosaurs and swimming plesiosaurs were different animal groups.
Some small dinosaurs were about the size of a chicken.
Scientists believe some dinosaurs could run as fast as 30 miles per hour.
Megalosaurus became the first dinosaur to be formally described by scientists, in 1824.
Deinonychus had a large, curved claw on the second toe of each foot.
Some long-necked dinosaurs, like Brachiosaurus, could reach leaves 30 feet (9 m) up in trees.
Fossilized dinosaur footprints can show scientists how fast a dinosaur was walking or running.
Microraptor was about the size of a crow and had long flight feathers on both its arms and legs.
Many dinosaurs laid eggs in nests, just like birds do today.
Some dinosaur fossils preserve feathers so finely that scientists can study their original color patterns.
Ankylosaurus had a giant bony club at the end of its tail for defense.
Some pterosaurs, flying reptiles from the dinosaur age, had wingspans as wide as a small airplane.
Some fossils preserve dinosaur skin impressions, revealing bumpy or scaly surfaces.
Compsognathus was a small dinosaur, about the size of a cat.
Many plant-eating dinosaurs had teeth adapted for grinding tough leaves.
Scientists think some dinosaurs may have been warm-blooded, more like birds than lizards.
Dinosaur trackways sometimes preserve many parallel paths, suggesting that the animals traveled together.
A Parasaurolophus had a long, curved crest on its head that may have made loud trumpeting sounds.
Dinosaur fossils include bones, teeth, eggs, footprints, skin impressions, and even feathers.

string-array.name: facts_nature_records
string-array.item: The tallest tree in the world, a redwood named Hyperion, is taller than a 30-story building.
Antarctica is the world\'s largest desert because deserts are defined by how little precipitation they receive.
The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth, covering more than 5.5 million square kilometers.
The Himalayas are still rising because the Indian tectonic plate continues to press into the Eurasian plate.
The Sahara Desert is almost as big as the entire United States.
Lightning can be five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
The Mariana Trench is so deep that Mount Everest could fit inside it with room to spare.
Thunder is the sound of air rapidly expanding after lightning heats it.
A honey fungus in Oregon forms one underground network across almost 4 square miles.
The Dead Sea is so salty that its dense water makes floating unusually easy.
A 253 mph (407 km/h) wind gust was recorded on Barrow Island during Tropical Cyclone Olivia in 1996.
Niagara Falls moves so much water that it could fill an Olympic swimming pool in about one second.
Snow crystals usually have six-fold symmetry because of the way water molecules arrange as they freeze.
Ground temperatures in Death Valley can rise above 200°F (93°C).
The Great Barrier Reef is the world\'s largest coral reef system and stretches for more than 1,400 miles (2,300 km).
A raindrop\'s falling speed depends on its size; large drops can reach about 20 mph (32 km/h).
Leaves of the giant water lily can grow more than 10 feet (3 m) across.
The Atacama Desert is so dry that some weather stations have gone decades without measurable rain.
Angel Falls, the world\'s tallest waterfall, has a total height of about 3,200 feet (979 m).
Some cave chambers are so vast that clouds can form inside them.
Glaciers and ice caps store about 69% of Earth\'s fresh water.
A rainbow is actually a full circle, but from the ground we usually see only an arc.
The lowest air temperature measured directly on Earth was about -128°F (-89°C) in Antarctica.
The Amazon River carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined.
Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants and can grow almost 3 feet (91 cm) in a single day.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in our solar system.
Some giant sequoias live for more than 3,000 years.
The Sahara Desert was once green and covered in lakes, thousands of years ago.
The largest hailstone measured in the United States was almost as wide as a volleyball.
Only about 10% of an iceberg rises above the water; the other 90% remains submerged.

string-array.name: facts_math
string-array.item: The traditional Roman numeral system has no symbol for zero.
A \"googol\" is 1 followed by 100 zeros, and its name inspired the name Google.
The infinity symbol (∞) has the shape of a curve called a \"lemniscate.\"
If you add up all the numbers from 1 to 100, you get 5,050.
A hexagon has exactly the same number of sides as it has angles: six.
For any positive multiple of 9, repeatedly adding its digits until one digit remains gives 9.
A Möbius strip has only one side and one edge.
Ancient Egyptians used fractions over 4,000 years ago to divide bread and land fairly.
A \"palindrome number,\" like 121 or 3443, reads the same forwards and backwards.
The equal sign (=) was invented in 1557 by a mathematician who was tired of writing \"is equal to.\"
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
The decimal form of pi (π) never ends or settles into a repeating pattern.
A \"baker\'s dozen\" means 13 instead of 12, an old tradition from bakers giving one extra item.
You can multiply by 5 quickly by multiplying by 10 and then dividing by 2.
A prime number has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself.
A googolplex is 1 followed by a googol of zeros — a number too big to even write out!
Ancient Babylonians counted using a base-60 number system, which is why we have 60 minutes in an hour.
Any number multiplied by zero always equals zero — no matter how big the number is!
An abacus, one of the earliest calculating tools, is still used to teach math today.
The angles of a triangle on a flat surface add up to exactly 180 degrees.
In many sunflower heads, the numbers of clockwise and counterclockwise spirals match consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
Mathematicians in ancient India developed rules for calculating with zero as a number.
Goldbach\'s conjecture says every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes, but no one has proved it yet.
The plus sign (+) is thought to come from an old shorthand way of writing the Latin word \"et,\" meaning \"and.\"
A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
Zero is neither positive nor negative.
A \"perfect number,\" like 6 or 28, equals the sum of its smaller positive divisors; for example, 1+2+3=6.
The multiplication sign (×) was first used in print in the year 1631.
Timekeeping still groups units by 12 and 60 instead of using only groups of 10.
A square number is what you get when you multiply a number by itself, like 4×4=16.
